power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Power to detect these shared effects, however, differed substantially between ancestries because of differences in allele frequency. Of the 7.0 million genetic variants shared between the EA and AA analysis, 637,000 shared variants differ in MAF by ≥0.2 between ancestries (e.g., MAFEA of 5% and MAFAA of 25% or vice versa). For a sample size of 800 and effect size of 0.4, increasing the MAF from 0.05 to 0.25 would increase the power to detect this effect size from 2.5% to 93% (37-fold gain in power; Fig. 4a). In addition, there were 1.5 million and 7.9 million variants unique to the EA and AA analysis, respectively (Fig. 4a). At index variants of EA-discovered mQTLs, minor allele frequencies were systematically higher in AA than in EA (serum: P = 0.006; urine: P = 2.2 × 10⁻⁴). The same pattern held for index variants of AAdiscovered mQTLs (serum: P = 7.7×10⁻⁵; urine: P = 1.1×10⁻⁹; Fig. 4c). In other words, mQTLs . identified in either ancestry tended to sit at variants that are more common in AA, consistent with statistical power rather than ancestry-specific biology driving ancestry-specificity.
table.header: Integrating European American and African American Ancestry Data to Enhance Genetic Discovery

table.text: UNC93A was recently nominated, by a machine-learning screen of orphan solute carriers, as a candidate transporter for acetylglucosamine; cells overexpressing UNC93A showed markedly increased cellular acetylglucosamine uptake, functionally supporting this candidacy, and its genetic association with circulating acetylglucosamine had previously been reported in European-ancestry cohorts. 34 In our data, the effect allele is common in both ancestries (AA: 17.6%; EA: 10.7%) and shows a strong, GCKD-replicated association with serum Nacetylglucosamine/N-acetylgalactosamine in EA (β = 0.455, P = 4.84 × 10⁻³⁵), yet no association at all in AA (β = -0.008, P = 0.89, adequately powered at N = 818). Finemapping resolves the locus to a single variant (PIP > 0.999), making differential linkage disequilibrium an unlikely explanation for this heterogeneity; a genuine gene-by-ancestry or gene-by-environment interaction is more plausible, though distinguishing between these would require direct functional follow-up. Dietary or microbiome-driven differences in circulating acetylglucosamine are one possible explanation that warrants further investigation. UNC93A thus illustrates how population-specific genetic regulation can be layered onto a transporter whose basic substrate biology has only just been established.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. table.header: Allele-frequency differences rather than selection underlie most ancestry differentiation
table.expanded: To our knowledge, no published genome-wide scans have reported evidence of positive selection at this locus (Fst = 0.062, 76th genome-wide percentile, empirical P = 0.24), and the observed frequency difference most likely reflects drift rather than adaptive divergence.

table.formatted: UNC93A was recently nominated, by a machine-learning screen of orphan solute carriers, as a candidate transporter for acetylglucosamine; cells overexpressing UNC93A showed markedly increased cellular acetylglucosamine uptake, functionally supporting this candidacy, and its genetic association with circulating acetylglucosamine had previously been reported in European-ancestry cohorts. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> In our data, the effect allele is common in both ancestries (AA: 17.6%; EA: 10.7%) and shows a strong, GCKD-replicated association with serum Nacetylglucosamine/N-acetylgalactosamine in EA (β = 0.455, P = 4.84 × 10⁻³⁵), yet no association at all in AA (β = -0.008, P = 0.89, adequately powered at N = 818).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: R history (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

live_data_statements: The participants were on average 76 years old, with a mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 72 mL/min/1.73m² (serum) and 66 mL/min/1.73m² (urine), and clinical characteristics were comparable across ancestry-by-biofluid strata (Supplementary Table 1).
Second, ARIC participants were older adults sampled at a single visit, ancestry groups were defined by self-report, and the cohort does not capture the full spectrum of human genetic diversity.
Participants were stratified by self-reported race/ethnicity into European American (EA) and African American (AA) ancestry groups.

text.text: European-ancestry populations using a single biofluid, constraining both the discovery of metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) and the resolution of causal variant finemapping.

Here, we report a multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of 1,955 serum and urine metabolites in 4,431 European American and African American participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study.
We identify 969 mQTLs for 553 metabolites, 30% unreported in studies of matched biofluid and ancestry, and replicate 91-99% of testable mQTLs in two independent cohorts.
In the African American sample with balanced sample sizes, 36% of metabolites with mQTLs are serum-specific, 39% urine-specific, and 25% shared, demonstrating complementary genetic architecture.

Only 23 of 632 candidate ancestryspecific mQTLs show heterogeneous effects beyond variant availability and power, yet allele frequency differences expose functional variants such as an SLC28A1 splice variant, virtually absent in Europeans, that increases urine uridine excretion, implicating impaired CNT1mediated renal nucleoside reabsorption.

Multi-ancestry finemapping improves credible set resolution, and colocalization with the Million Veteran Program phenome links the catalog to cardiometabolic, kidney and liver traits consistent with prioritized gene function.
Integrating biofluids and ancestries enhances genetic discovery and mechanistic characterization of the human metabolome.
Genome-wide association studies of the metabolome (mGWAS) connect genetic variation to small-molecule levels, and thereby to the enzymes and transporters that produce, convert and clear them.

Targeted nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) panels such as Nightingale quantify about 250 predominantly lipoprotein, lipid, fatty-acid, amino-acid and glycolysisrelated traits in up to 619,372 individuals. 1, 2 Untargeted mass-spectrometry panels such as Metabolon resolve more than a thousand molecules, including amino acids, lipids, nucleotides, xenobiotics, and unnamed compounds. [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] The strongest signals typically fall in genes whose products act directly on the associated metabolite, 8, 9 such as the desaturase FADS1 for polyunsaturated phospholipids, and the transporter SLC16A9 for carnitine and urate 10 .

text.text: Because such loci often also associate with disease, metabolites can point to candidate causal genes at disease loci and pose a mechanistic hypothesis for experimental validation.

Joint profiling of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma proteomes has led to major advances 11 in neurological disease, and CSF metabolomics has proven similarly complementary to blood. 12 For metabolomics, most efforts have focused on serum or plasma, 1, 8, 13 leaving the urine metabolome, which reflects renal handling and xenobiotic clearance, underinvestigated despite a growing number of efforts. 7, 14 Paired plasma and urine mGWAS have revealed enzymatic and transport processes at their interface, motivating joint modeling. 14 Moreover, the metabolome has been mapped in only a few multi-ancestry mGWAS. 1, 15, 16 Multi-ancestry designs exploit differences in allele frequency and linkage disequilibrium (LD) to increase power and finemapping resolution, as the Million Veteran Program (MVP) showed for both variant discovery and credible set resolution. 17 Participants of African American as well as African ancestry remain severely underrepresented in GWAS and mGWAS efforts to date with few exceptions [18] [19] [20] , despite the greater genetic diversity and shorter LD blocks on average in African American ancestry populations, and no Metabolon-based urine mGWAS in African American participants has been reported.

We conducted a multi-ancestry mGWAS of the serum and urine metabolome in participants of EA and AA ancestry with available genotype data and metabolomic profiling from visit 5 (2011-2013) from the ARIC study (serum: 3,607 EA / 818 AA; urine: 797 EA / 794 AA; both biofluids: 1,585; Supplementary Table 1; Extended Data Fig. 1).

text.text: The participants were on average 76 years old, with a mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 72 mL/min/1.73m² (serum) and 66 mL/min/1.73m² (urine), and clinical characteristics were comparable across ancestry-by-biofluid strata (Supplementary Table 1).

text.text: After stringent quality control, 1,316 serum and 1,374 urine metabolites, harmonized to 1,955 unique analytes, were analyzed within each stratum (Methods; Supplementary Table 2).

Effect directions were consistent in the other biofluid for 88% (EA) and 90% (AA) of mQTLs measured in both (Supplementary Tables 3 4).

The index variant explained a median of 10.7% of metabolite variance (Q1-Q3: 6.6-15.7%).

14.2%; Methods).
Of the 1,955 unique metabolites 581 were only detected in serum, 639 only in urine, and 735 in both biofluids with overall aligned effect sizes across biofluids in both ancestries (Fig. 2a,b).

text.text: Among the metabolites measured in both biofluids, 41 exhibited biofluid-specific mQTLs, which would have been missed if only one biofluid had been analyzed.

This aligns with the proportions previously reported for an EA cohort, 7 highlighting the specific value of urinary metabolite quantification and, more broadly, the importance of conducting multi-biofluid molecular GWAS. 14 The increased statistical power from larger serum sample size in EA shifted proportions accordingly (76% serum only, 12% urine only, 13% both; Extended Data Fig. 3).

text.text: To test whether this shift reflects power, we repeated the EA serum mGWAS in the 797 EA participants with paired urine measurements (Supplementary Tables 6-7; Methods).

At matched sample size, the serum-specific proportion fell from 76% to 35%, urine-specific rose from 12% to 45%, and shared rose from 13% to 21%; the serum:urine mQTL ratio fell from 4.5:1 to 0.8:1, i.e. urine yielded more mQTLs than serum at equal N (Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 8).

text.text: All 115 power-matched mQTLs were recovered within 1 Mb of the original full-sample serum signals (median distance 4.4 kb), supporting that down-sampling reduces power without introducing spurious loci.

These results indicate that the apparent predominance of serum-specific signals in the EA stratum reflects statistical power rather than biofluid-specific biology, and that at equal sample size urine is at least as informative as serum.

Of the three available in EA, two showed large MAF differences: 3beta,7alpha-dihydroxy-5-cholestenoate at HSD3B7 (31% in AA vs 1% in EA) and 3methoxytyrosine at DDC (15% in AA vs 1% in EA).
The remaining variant, associated with N6methyllysine at LCOR, had a comparable MAF in both ancestries (16% in AA vs 19% in EA).

A notable example illustrating the impact of ancestry differences in allele frequency on mQTL discovery is the missense variant rs37369 (chr5:35037010:C:T; NM_031900.4:c.418G>A, p.Val140Ile) in AGXT2, encoding alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase 2.

text.text: This variant was associated with 3-aminoisobutyrate levels across both biofluids in EA, where both associations were classified as shared between ancestries because of an AA mQTL within the 1 Mb window.

In total, 3-aminoisobutyrate had three serum mQTLs (1 EA-AA shared, 1 candidate EA-specific) and two urine mQTLs (1 AA-EA shared) of which only the candidate EA-specific was not annotated to AGXT2 but rather to SLC6A13.

The effect allele (T, derived allele) frequency of rs37369 differs markedly between populations, at approximately 8% in EA and 55% in AA, with substantial global variation reported across diverse populations.

To our knowledge, no published genome-wide scans have reported evidence of positive selection at this locus (Fst = 0.062, 76th genome-wide percentile, empirical P = 0.24), and the observed frequency difference most likely reflects drift rather than adaptive divergence.

This frequency disparity . has direct consequences for statistical power: while the variant reached genome-wide significance for 3-aminoisobutyrate in EA in both biofluids, the weaker serum effect failed to reach significance in AA, and the urine association was only marginally genome-wide significant (P ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁹).
The variant replicated in GCKD, where the effect allele frequency (~8%) closely mirrors that of ARIC EA, consistent with the European ancestry of that cohort.

In the locus-level classification, the 3-aminoisobutyrate mQTLs at AGXT2 are shared between ancestries in both biofluids (Supplementary Tables 3 4), so the frequency difference modulates power at a shared locus rather than marking metabolite handling that works differently between ancestries.

text.text: A contrasting case is the UNC93A locus (chr6:167294271:C:T), one of the 23 loci that remain ancestry-specific after the classification above and also a fine-mapped ancestry-specific signal.

UNC93A was recently nominated, by a machine-learning screen of orphan solute carriers, as a candidate transporter for acetylglucosamine; cells overexpressing UNC93A showed markedly increased cellular acetylglucosamine uptake, functionally supporting this candidacy, and its genetic association with circulating acetylglucosamine had previously been reported in European-ancestry cohorts. 34 In our data, the effect allele is common in both ancestries (AA: 17.6%; EA: 10.7%) and shows a strong, GCKD-replicated association with serum Nacetylglucosamine/N-acetylgalactosamine in EA (β = 0.455, P = 4.84 × 10⁻³⁵), yet no association at all in AA (β = -0.008, P = 0.89, adequately powered at N = 818).

UNC93A thus illustrates how population-specific genetic regulation can be layered onto a transporter whose basic substrate biology has only just been established.
We next asked whether the frequency differentials extend across the mQTL catalog, using Fst between reference populations as a measure of allele-frequency differentiation (Methods).

Fst was available for 609 of 969 index variants (63%, Supplementary Tables 3 4); for each, we report its percentile in the genome-wide Fst distribution, i.e., the share of all variants that are less differentiated between CEU and YRI.

text.text: Differentiation is only modestly elevated overall (mean percentile 57.9; 9.0% of variants in the top 5% of the genome-wide distribution, against . 5% expected).
Index variants of mQTLs identified in African American participants sit at a higher mean percentile than those identified in European American participants (66.1 vs.
55.9), driven mainly by signals shared across ancestries (69.2) rather than those specific to African American participants (54.7).

Because allele-frequency differentiation can arise from drift as well as from selection, these data indicate at most a weak, nonpervasive contribution of population-differentiating selection to the frequency differentials described above.

text.text: VEP annotated the majority as MODIFIER impact (87.2%), consistent with their predominantly non-coding genomic context.
Notably, 9.4% of finemapped SNVs were classified as missense, and 0.8% of all variants carried HIGH impact consequences, including splice donor variants.

The proportion of HIGH impact variants was highest among indels (4.3%), followed by SNVs (0.4%), with a background rate of 0.0%, highlighting the potential of multi-ancestry-based statistical finemapping to prioritize functionally consequential variants.

To complement categorical annotation with quantitative predictions of regulatory impact, we scored all finemapped variants using AlphaGenome, 36 a deep learning model that predicts molecular effects across chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding, histone . modification, and gene expression tracks in hundreds of cell types (Supplementary Tables 22 and 24).

text.text: A total of 251 variants (33.1%) showed predicted disruption of at least one transcription factor binding site in any tissue.

Several established regulators of hepatic and renal gene expression were among the most frequently disrupted transcription factors: SP1 (53 variants, 21.1% of TF-hit variants), CEBPB (43, 17.1%), RXRA and FOXA1 (35 each, 13.9%), FOXA2 (32, 12.7%), and HNF4A (25, 10.0%).

Of these, HNF4A, FOXA1, FOXA2, and RXRA are liver-enriched transcription factors that cooperatively regulate metabolic gene programs in liver and kidney 37, 38 , while SP1 and CEBPB are broadly expressed transcription factors with known roles in hepatic gene regulation 39, 40 .

text.text: When restricting to metabolically relevant tissues (Methods), kidney was the most frequent top organ (228 of 687 annotated variants, 33.2%), followed by liver (176, 25.6%), consistent with the renal and hepatic origin of many circulating and urinary metabolites.
Among the 251 unique high-PIP variants with predicted transcription factor binding disruption, 25 (10.0%) were predicted to affect HNF4A binding in primary liver tissue or HepG2.
HNF4A is of particular biological interest given its established role as a master regulator of hepatic lipid and fatty acid metabolism.

One such variant, chr11:61820833:A:G (rs174564), annotated by VEP as an upstream gene variant of FADS1 on chromosome 11, disrupts a predicted HNF4A binding site in liver and appeared in credible sets for 17 serum metabolites spanning phosphatidylcholines, plasmalogens, diacylglycerols, and free arachidonate -all substrates or products of the FADS1/2 desaturation pathway.

For ten of these metabolites, the variant was the sole member of the credible set (PIP > 0.96, Supplementary Table 22), making it one of the most confidently finemapped multi-metabolite variants in our study.

This locus illustrates directly how multi-ancestry finemapping improves resolution: for this metabolite, the EA association is exceptionally strong (P = 6.98 × 10⁻¹³⁰) but falls within a broad region of high linkage disequilibrium, with several correlated variants reaching comparably high significance and no single candidate resolved when EA is considered alone.

The AA association, while considerably weaker (P = 1.67 × 10⁻¹⁴), shows a more localized pattern around the same variant; jointly modeling both ancestries with MESuSiE collapses the credible set to this single variant (PIP > 0.999), despite AA's lower power (Fig. 6b).

text.text: This locus also showed the broadest disease colocalization in our catalog (see below).

The ALDH7A1 locus on chromosome 5 illustrates how combining multi-ancestry finemapping with deep learning-based functional prediction can strengthen the case for follow-up of individual mQTL variants.

Two mQTL regions were identified for serum levels of 6oxopiperidine-2-carboxylate, a key intermediate in lysine catabolism, which accumulates in the plasma and urine of patients with ALDH7A1 deficiency: a shared signal at the OPLAH locus and an EA-specific signal at ALDH7A1 on chromosome 5, encoding aldehyde dehydrogenase 7 family member A1.

At the ALDH7A1 locus, the index variant was not represented in the 1000 Genomes CEU/YRI reference panel and therefore lacks an Fst estimate, consistent with its . classification as a candidate ancestry-specific signal driven by variant unavailability in EA.

The EA association was strong (β = 0.54, P = 6.45 x 10 -19 , N = 3,595) whereas no significant signal was detected in AA (β = 0.28, P = 0.31, N = 811), consistent with a pronounced allele frequency difference (EAFEA = 0.04 vs.
EAFAA = 0.01).
Finemapping identified a single credible set of five variants with a cumulative coverage probability of 0.97.
The top variant chr5:126595258:C:T carried a PIP of 0.52.
This variant is also the EA index variant for the locus (Extended Data Fig 10a).
text.formatted: This variant is also the EA index variant for the locus (Extended Data Fig <ref type="figure">10a</ref>).

text.text: Finemapping classified the credible set as EA-specific, underscoring how the multiancestry framework helps delineate ancestry-dependent genetic architecture even when one stratum contributes minimal information for finemapping above LD patterns.
VEP annotated the variant as an upstream gene variant (CADD PHRED score 18.8).
The variant is classified as benign/likely benign in ClinVar with respect to Mendelian disease, consistent with its role as a common regulatory variant rather than a disease-causing allele.
AlphaGenome predicted tissue-differential regulatory disruption across multiple functional modalities.

In the ChIP-TF output, the alternate allele was associated with reduced predicted binding of RNA Polymerase II (POLR2A) across 42 biosamples, as well as diminished binding of liver-relevant transcription factors including SP1, FOXA1, FOXA2, and RXRA (Supplementary Table 22).
text.formatted: In the ChIP-TF output, the alternate allele was associated with reduced predicted binding of RNA Polymerase II (POLR2A) across 42 biosamples, as well as diminished binding of liver-relevant transcription factors including SP1, FOXA1, FOXA2, and RXRA (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">22</ref>).

text.text: Notably, the predicted effect on the H3K4me3 active promoter mark was tissue-dependent: in K562, the variant was associated with a pronounced loss of H3K4me3 at the ALDH7A1 promoter, whereas in liver and kidney -the primary tissues of ALDH7A1 expression and lysine catabolism -H3K4me3 was predicted to increase (Extended Data Fig. 10b).
text.formatted: Notably, the predicted effect on the H3K4me3 active promoter mark was tissue-dependent: in K562, the variant was associated with a pronounced loss of H3K4me3 at the ALDH7A1 promoter, whereas in liver and kidney -the primary tissues of ALDH7A1 expression and lysine catabolism -H3K4me3 was predicted to increase (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">10b</ref>).

text.text: By contrast, AlphaGenome predicted uniformly reduced DNase-seq accessibility at the variant site across all three tissues, suggesting that the variant alters chromatin accessibility broadly but exerts tissue-specific effects on promoter histone modifications.

The H3K4me3 gain in liver and kidney suggests that the variant may enhance promoter activity at ALDH7A1 specifically in tissues central to lysine catabolism, consistent with the serum-specific mQTL association observed for its downstream product 6-oxopiperidine-2-carboxylate.

Taken together, the convergence of a moderate-PIP finemapping signal with consistent, tissue-specific epigenomic disruption predicted by AlphaGenome supports chr5:126595258:C:T (ALDH7A1:c.-60G>T, a 5 prime UTR variant) as a high-priority candidate for experimental follow-up to understand the metabolic block in lysine catabolism, and illustrates how deep learning-based variant effect prediction can add functional confidence to statistically ambiguous finemapping results.

text.text: To link our mQTL catalog to diseases and clinical outcomes, we conducted colocalization analysis to test whether each locus shares a causal variant with 3,037 trait-ancestry outcomes from the Million Veteran Program (MVP) phenome-wide GWAS (Methods). 17 At a posterior probability of a shared causal variant (PP.H4) > 0.8, we detected colocalizations for 521 metabolite-stratum pairs (381 unique metabolites) across 125 genes and 217 MVP trait families spanning 12 disease categories (Supplementary Table 25).
text.formatted: To link our mQTL catalog to diseases and clinical outcomes, we conducted colocalization analysis to test whether each locus shares a causal variant with 3,037 trait-ancestry outcomes from the Million Veteran Program (MVP) phenome-wide GWAS (Methods). <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> At a posterior probability of a shared causal variant (PP.H4) > 0.8, we detected colocalizations for 521 metabolite-stratum pairs (381 unique metabolites) across 125 genes and 217 MVP trait families spanning 12 disease categories (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">25</ref>).

text.text: Quantitative traits dominated, led by serum triglycerides (182 metabolite-stratum pairs, 28 genes) and eGFR (181 metabolite-stratum pairs, 23 genes).

Among binary outcomes, the strongest metabolite-level signals were gout (70 metabolite-stratum pairs, 12 genes), hyperlipidemia (73, 11), chronic kidney disease (74, 4), liver-function abnormalities (63, 6) and hypercholesterolemia (57, 14).
The implicated diseases matched the known physiology of the prioritized genes.
Genes involved in lipid transport and metabolism colocalized with triglycerides, cholesterol and hyperlipidemia (e.g.
ALDH1A2, UGT1A1); kidney-expressed transporters and enzymes with creatinine, eGFR and chronic kidney disease (e.g.
NAT8); and urate-handling loci with gout (e.g.
ABCG2, SLC22A5, GCKR).

The most broadly connected genes were FADS1, a fatty-acid desaturase (31 metabolite-stratum pairs, 63 trait families spanning lipid, cardiovascular and inflammatory traits), whose signal multi-ancestry finemapping resolved to a single candidate variant (see above); SLCO1B1, a hepatic transporter of bile acids and statins (45 metabolitestratum pairs, 20 trait families including liver and lipid phenotypes); and CPS1, the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle (26 metabolite-stratum pairs, 13 families centered on kidney and nitrogen-handling traits).
That the diseases recovered for each gene consistently match its established function gives independent support to our gene prioritization, beyond metabolitelevel evidence alone.

A locus at ENPEP (aminopeptidase A, chr4:110.42-110.57 Mb), which cleaves angiotensin II in the renin-angiotensin system, colocalized with fibrinopeptide A degradation fragments (thrombin-cleavage products of fibrinogen, distinct from fibrinogen itself) and with blood pressure, hypertension and serum potassium traits (PP.H4 up to 1.00).

The lead variant, a rare stop-gain allele in ENPEP (rs33966350), has independently been shown to reduce kidney ENPEP expression and raise hypertension risk, 43 and an association between this same variant and fibrinopeptide A fragments has been reported in an Amish cohort 44 (Extended Data Fig. 11).
text.formatted: The lead variant, a rare stop-gain allele in ENPEP (rs33966350), has independently been shown to reduce kidney ENPEP expression and raise hypertension risk, <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> and an association between this same variant and fibrinopeptide A fragments has been reported in an Amish cohort <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">11</ref>).

text.text: We investigated this locus further with complementary medication-based observational analyses in ARIC (Methods, Supplementary Note 2, Extended Data Fig 11).
text.formatted: We investigated this locus further with complementary medication-based observational analyses in ARIC (Methods, Supplementary Note 2, Extended Data Fig <ref type="figure">11</ref>).

text.text: These indicate that genetically or pharmacologically reduced ACE activity specifically alters fibrinopeptide fragment levels.
ACE-inhibitor use (but not angiotensin-receptor-blocker use) reproduces this pattern (e.g.

FPB(1-13), P = 2 × 10⁻²⁹⁶) and in a mechanistically coherent direction, while clinical coagulation markers (fibrinogen, APTT, von Willebrand factor), available only from earlier study visits, did not differ between later ACE-inhibitor users and untreated participants in the same cohort.

A plausible explanation is that ACE continues to act on the fibrinopeptide substrate pool generated during clot formation within the serum sample tube, similar in principle to a synthetic-substrate ACE activity assay, so that ACE genotype and ACE-inhibitor status at the time of blood draw are reflected in these measurements alongside any physiological signal.

A second locus, at SLC16A9 (MCT9, a renal carnitine/urate transporter, chr10:59.67-59.71 Mb), colocalized with serum acylcarnitines, urate-related traits (gout, PP.H4 up to 0.998) and coronary atherosclerosis (PP.H4 up to 0.997) simultaneously (Extended Data Fig. 12).
text.formatted: A second locus, at SLC16A9 (MCT9, a renal carnitine/urate transporter, chr10:59.67-59.71 Mb), colocalized with serum acylcarnitines, urate-related traits (gout, PP.H4 up to 0.998) and coronary atherosclerosis (PP.H4 up to 0.997) simultaneously (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">12</ref>).

text.text: A carnitine-mediated mechanism was biologically plausible a priori: MCT9 mediates carnitine efflux in a context-dependent manner, 45 and altered cellular carnitine handling could affect mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation and acylcarnitine accumulation, both previously linked to cardiac lipotoxicity.
text.formatted: A carnitine-mediated mechanism was biologically plausible a priori: MCT9 mediates carnitine efflux in a context-dependent manner, <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> and altered cellular carnitine handling could affect mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation and acylcarnitine accumulation, both previously linked to cardiac lipotoxicity.

text.text: Mendelian randomization (Methods, Supplementary Note 3) supported a causal effect of urate on gout and, less robustly, on coronary artery disease (significant with the inverse-variance-weighted and weighted-median estimators but not with MR-Egger), mirroring previous Mendelian randomization analyses of urate and coronary heart disease. 46 At this locus, the carnitine-and urate-transport signals were not statistically separable, so the coronary colocalization cannot be attributed to carnitine (see Discussion).
text.formatted: Mendelian randomization (Methods, Supplementary Note 3) supported a causal effect of urate on gout and, less robustly, on coronary artery disease (significant with the inverse-variance-weighted and weighted-median estimators but not with MR-Egger), mirroring previous Mendelian randomization analyses of urate and coronary heart disease. <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> At this locus, the carnitine-and urate-transport signals were not statistically separable, so the coronary colocalization cannot be attributed to carnitine (see Discussion).

text.text: A genome-wide gout instrument was similarly associated with coronary artery disease, but showed directional pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept test), likely reflecting that a case-control gout diagnosis captures broader inflammatory/comorbidity-driven biology beyond urate handling, rather than a clean urate-specific signal.

Our multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of paired serum and urine metabolomes in the ARIC cohort represents, to our knowledge, the first systematic investigation combining . ancestrally diverse populations with multi-biofluid metabolite profiling.

We identified 969 mQTLs for 553 metabolites, replicated them in GCKD and, for urine mQTLs in the African American stratum, de novo in CRIC, and linked 521 metabolite-stratum pairs to clinical traits through colocalization with the MVP phenome.
Three findings stand out.
Serum and urine capture complementary genetic regulation that is not explained by sample size.

Most ancestry-differentiated signals reflect allele frequency and power rather than ancestryspecific metabolite handling, yet frequency differences expose functional variants such as the SLC28A1 splice variant.
Multi-ancestry finemapping and colocalization together prioritize enzymes and transporters whose disease links match their physiology.
The contribution of this catalog does not rest on locus counts alone.

Looking at biofluid-and ancestry-matched studies using Metabolon, 30% of our mQTLs are not reported before, rising to 100% in the urine African American stratum, where no comparable prior resource exists, and 9% remain unreported even when a report in any biofluid or ancestry or platform is counted as prior knowledge.

What cannot be obtained by combining the existing literature is the design itself: paired serum and urine metabolomes measured in the same individuals, a combination only GCKD also provides, and only in a chronic-kidney-disease population, together with a substantial African American component in both biofluids, for which essentially no prior Metabolon urine resource exists.
The complementary nature of serum and urine metabolome profiling was a central finding of our study.

In the African American cohort, where sample sizes were balanced across biofluids, we observed that 36% of metabolites with mQTLs had associations detectable only in serum, 39% only in urine, and 25% in both biofluids.

This distribution aligns with proportions previously reported in the GCKD study, which demonstrated that urine metabolomics can reveal genetic associations invisible to studies focusing solely on circulating metabolites. 14 The apparent serum predominance in European Americans disappeared at matched sample size, and other studies recovered our mQTLs far more often within than across biofluids (urine: 85% versus 53%; serum: 91% versus 31%), directly quantifying how much biofluid-specific effects a single-biofluid design would miss.
text.formatted: This distribution aligns with proportions previously reported in the GCKD study, which demonstrated that urine metabolomics can reveal genetic associations invisible to studies focusing solely on circulating metabolites. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> The apparent serum predominance in European Americans disappeared at matched sample size, and other studies recovered our mQTLs far more often within than across biofluids (urine: 85% versus 53%; serum: 91% versus 31%), directly quantifying how much biofluid-specific effects a single-biofluid design would miss.

text.text: These differences follow from physiology.
Circulating levels integrate hepatic synthesis, conjugation and uptake, whereas urinary levels additionally reflect glomerular filtration and tubular secretion and reabsorption.

Consistent with this, mQTL genes were enriched for liver and kidney expression; serum-only pathways centred on xenobiotic processing, lipid and fatty . acid metabolism and bile secretion; and glutathione and butanoate metabolism were enriched only in urine, while glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism showed its strongest enrichment in urine, pointing to renal tubular metabolism.

A variant in a tubular transporter can therefore leave a large urinary signal with a smaller change in blood, as at SLC28A1, where the effect allele raised urinary uridine and 2'-O-methyluridine but lowered serum cytidine.
The AA-specific enrichment of uracil-containing pyrimidine metabolites, upstream of beta-alanine, points to further regulation that single-ancestry studies would miss.
A key motivation for our multi-ancestry design was to leverage the genetic diversity present in African American populations to improve finemapping precision.

African American populations exhibit shorter linkage disequilibrium (LD) blocks and greater genetic diversity compared to European populations, features that have been shown to substantially improve the resolution of credible sets in finemapping analyses. 35 The Million Veteran Program has demonstrated that multi-ancestry approaches can identify population-specific causal variants and narrow credible sets relative to European-only analyses. 17 Consistent with these expectations, our multi-ancestry MESuSiE finemapping detected more independent signals than single-ancestry SuSiE, and the African American-specific signals yielded the most specific credible sets.
text.formatted: African American populations exhibit shorter linkage disequilibrium (LD) blocks and greater genetic diversity compared to European populations, features that have been shown to substantially improve the resolution of credible sets in finemapping analyses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> The Million Veteran Program has demonstrated that multi-ancestry approaches can identify population-specific causal variants and narrow credible sets relative to European-only analyses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> Consistent with these expectations, our multi-ancestry MESuSiE finemapping detected more independent signals than single-ancestry SuSiE, and the African American-specific signals yielded the most specific credible sets.

text.text: Even in serum, where European American sample sizes were 4.4-fold larger, incorporating African American data improved credible set resolution, as at FADS1, where the joint model resolved a signal that European-ancestry data alone could not.
Ancestry-differentiated discovery was largely a matter of allele frequency.

Of 632 candidate ancestry-specific mQTLs, only 23 (4%) showed heterogeneous effects once variant availability and power were accounted for, and index variants discovered in either ancestry were systematically more common in African Americans.

Population differentiation (Fst) at index variants was only modestly elevated and higher at ancestry-shared than at candidate ancestry-specific loci among African American, arguing against widespread selection.
Diverse cohorts therefore reveal biology that is shared across ancestries but detectable only where the relevant allele is common, as at SLC28A1, or that modulate power at shared loci such as AGXT2.
Genuine heterogeneity, as at UNC93A, was rare and may reflect gene-by-environment interactions, for example through diet or the microbiome.
Among loci shared across ancestries, the AGXT2/rs37369 region exemplifies how multiancestry mQTL mapping can illuminate population-specific variants with clinical relevance.

The variant rs37369 has previously been identified as the genetic basis of hyper-beta-. aminoisobutyric aciduria in a previous urine metabolomics GWAS, 9 and subsequent work has confirmed that AGXT2 polymorphisms, including this variant, have considerable impact on both methylarginine and beta-aminoisobutyrate metabolism.
text.formatted: The variant rs37369 has previously been identified as the genetic basis of hyper-beta-. aminoisobutyric aciduria in a previous urine metabolomics GWAS, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> and subsequent work has confirmed that AGXT2 polymorphisms, including this variant, have considerable impact on both methylarginine and beta-aminoisobutyrate metabolism.

text.text: Beyond metabolomics, the variant and the AGXT2 locus have been implicated in blood pressure regulation, 47 coronary artery disease risk, and chronic heart failure 48 , with several of these findings originating from East Asian populations where the effect allele frequency more closely resembles that observed in AA than in EA.
text.formatted: Beyond metabolomics, the variant and the AGXT2 locus have been implicated in blood pressure regulation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> coronary artery disease risk, and chronic heart failure <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> , with several of these findings originating from East Asian populations where the effect allele frequency more closely resembles that observed in AA than in EA.

text.text: The pleiotropic involvement of AGXT2 in both metabolite handling and cardiorenal phenotypes, combined with the pronounced population-level allele frequency variation at this locus, underscores the importance of multi-ancestry study designs for comprehensive mQTL characterization.
The SLC28A1 locus exemplifies the power of multi-ancestry approaches to identify functional variants with population-specific effects.

We detected an African Amercian-enriched splicedisrupting variant associated with urinary 2'-O-methyluridine levels -a signal that would have been missed entirely in European-ancestry-only studies due to the near-absence of this allele in European populations.

SLC28A1 encodes the concentrative nucleoside transporter CNT1, a sodium-dependent pyrimidine nucleoside transporter highly expressed in kidney tubular epithelium. 49 Our genetic findings provide human evidence for the potential role of SLC28A1 in methylated nucleoside transport, validating and extending observations from Slc28a1knockout mice. 32 The conserved metabolic phenotype across species underlines its physiological importance.
text.formatted: SLC28A1 encodes the concentrative nucleoside transporter CNT1, a sodium-dependent pyrimidine nucleoside transporter highly expressed in kidney tubular epithelium. <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49</ref> Our genetic findings provide human evidence for the potential role of SLC28A1 in methylated nucleoside transport, validating and extending observations from Slc28a1knockout mice. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> The conserved metabolic phenotype across species underlines its physiological importance.

text.text: The functional consequences of SLC28A1 loss have been characterized in both human disease and mouse models.

Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in SLC28A1 cause uridine-cytidinuria, an inborn error of metabolism characterized by elevated urinary excretion of pyrimidine nucleosides. 33 Supporting our findings, metabolomic profiling of Slc28a1-knockout mice demonstrated elevated urinary excretion of both canonical pyrimidines and methylated pyrimidine derivatives, suggesting that modified nucleosides derived from tRNA and rRNA degradation are also low-affinity substrates of this transporter. 32 Our observation that the African American-specific splice variant was associated with both increased urinary 2'-Omethyluridine, urinary uridine and reduced serum cytidine levels is consistent with impaired tubular reabsorption of pyrimidine nucleosides.
text.formatted: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in SLC28A1 cause uridine-cytidinuria, an inborn error of metabolism characterized by elevated urinary excretion of pyrimidine nucleosides. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> Supporting our findings, metabolomic profiling of Slc28a1-knockout mice demonstrated elevated urinary excretion of both canonical pyrimidines and methylated pyrimidine derivatives, suggesting that modified nucleosides derived from tRNA and rRNA degradation are also low-affinity substrates of this transporter. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> Our observation that the African American-specific splice variant was associated with both increased urinary 2'-Omethyluridine, urinary uridine and reduced serum cytidine levels is consistent with impaired tubular reabsorption of pyrimidine nucleosides.

text.text: Whether methylated nucleosides are direct CNT1 substrates (consistent with CNT1's established capacity to transport structurally modified nucleoside analogues) or accumulate secondarily to elevated parental nucleoside . pools and downstream modification cannot be distinguished from association data alone.
The supporting evidence from a liver-specific splice-QTL in GTEx 50 strengthens the case for this variant's functional impact.

This finding may have broader implications for pharmacogenomics, as CNT1 is involved in the disposition of nucleoside analog drugs, including gemcitabine and other antineoplastic and antiviral agents. 51 Population-specific functional variants in drug transporters may contribute to inter-individual variability in therapeutic response and toxicity, highlighting the importance of including diverse populations in both basic science and translational research.
text.formatted: This finding may have broader implications for pharmacogenomics, as CNT1 is involved in the disposition of nucleoside analog drugs, including gemcitabine and other antineoplastic and antiviral agents. <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51</ref> Population-specific functional variants in drug transporters may contribute to inter-individual variability in therapeutic response and toxicity, highlighting the importance of including diverse populations in both basic science and translational research.

text.text: Our use of TOPMed-based imputation contributed importantly to our results. 52 The TOPMed reference panel, with its substantial inclusion of African and Hispanic/Latino individuals, provides superior imputation quality for non-European populations compared to earlier European-centric panels.
text.formatted: Our use of TOPMed-based imputation contributed importantly to our results. <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> The TOPMed reference panel, with its substantial inclusion of African and Hispanic/Latino individuals, provides superior imputation quality for non-European populations compared to earlier European-centric panels.

text.text: Notably, 58 (6%) of our mQTL index variants were insertions or deletions (indels), a class of variants that earlier imputation panels often failed to capture adequately.

Indels can have substantial functional consequences but have been underrepresented in GWAS catalogs; their detection in our study reflects both improved imputation and the use of metabolomics as a sensitive intermediate phenotype.
Colocalization with the MVP phenome extends the catalog from genetic loci to candidate disease mechanisms.

The implicated diseases consistently matched gene function: lipidhandling genes with dyslipidaemia, kidney-expressed transporters and enzymes with eGFR and chronic kidney disease, and urate-handling loci with gout.
Pleiotropic hubs such as FADS1, SLCO1B1 and CPS1 connect dozens of metabolites to many trait families, consistent with disease effects that act through the pathways these genes control.
Colocalization indicates a shared causal variant, however, not proof of a causal chain.
SLC16A9 illustrates this caveat.
The locus links acylcarnitines to gout and coronary atherosclerosis, and a carnitine-mediated effect on cardiac lipotoxicity was plausible a priori.
Mendelian randomization could not separate the carnitine-and urate-transport roles of SLC16A9, as expected for a single transporter carrying both substrates.

Our estimate for urate on coronary artery disease resembles earlier Mendelian randomization work: robust with conventional estimators but attenuated under MR-Egger. 46 Randomized trials of urate-lowering therapy have not reduced cardiovascular events in patients with ischemic heart disease 53 or improved outcomes in heart failure. 54 Nor did they slow atherosclerosis, measured either as carotid intima-media thickness 55 or as coronary plaque volume. 56 These trials started treatment late in life or after . disease onset and ran for months to a few years, whereas genetic variants act lifelong.

text.text: Additionally, these trials largely enrolled people without gout.

In gout, reaching a serum urate target below 6 mg/dL was associated with fewer major adverse cardiovascular events 57 , but this setting cannot distinguish an effect of urate from suppression of gout-related inflammation, and the exposure was defined by treatment response rather than assignment.
text.formatted: In gout, reaching a serum urate target below 6 mg/dL was associated with fewer major adverse cardiovascular events <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57</ref> , but this setting cannot distinguish an effect of urate from suppression of gout-related inflammation, and the exposure was defined by treatment response rather than assignment.

text.text: These results therefore do not exclude a contribution of urate to atherogenesis, but they argue against urate lowering as a cardiovascular intervention at least in the general population.
We therefore do not interpret the coronary colocalization at SLC16A9 as evidence of a modifiable urate-or carnitine-driven pathway.

Genetically predicted carnitine has been associated with higher coronary artery disease risk 58 , but those instruments include pleiotropic transporter loci, so a carnitine-mediated pathway remains a hypothesis.
text.formatted: Genetically predicted carnitine has been associated with higher coronary artery disease risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58</ref> , but those instruments include pleiotropic transporter loci, so a carnitine-mediated pathway remains a hypothesis.

text.text: We regard the locus as a robust statistical association whose precise causal pathway remains to be established.
ENPEP illustrates a different kind of insight.

Fibrinopeptides have been proposed as a marker of disseminated intravascular coagulation 59, 60 , but this has not become part of routine clinical practice, which instead typically measures fibrinogen or D-dimer directly.
text.formatted: Fibrinopeptides have been proposed as a marker of disseminated intravascular coagulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">60</ref> , but this has not become part of routine clinical practice, which instead typically measures fibrinogen or D-dimer directly.

text.text: Fibrinopeptides have also been explored as a marker of other thrombotic conditions 61 , raising the possibility of broader future diagnostic use.
text.formatted: Fibrinopeptides have also been explored as a marker of other thrombotic conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> , raising the possibility of broader future diagnostic use.

text.text: Our results indicate that measured levels of these fragments are shaped not only by a patient's coagulation state but also by their ACE-inhibitor treatment status and ENPEP/ACE genotype: ACE continues to act on the fibrinopeptide substrate pool generated during clot formation in the sample tube, so a patient's ACE activity at the time of blood draw is captured alongside, and potentially confounded with, any coagulation-related signal.

Should fibrinopeptide-based testing see wider clinical use, this would be a relevant consideration -and, conversely, these fragments could in principle serve as a biomarker of ACE-inhibitor activity itself.
The findings more broadly connect the renin-angiotensin and coagulation systems.
Cross-study replication in metabolomics is bounded by platform comparability.

NMR panels such as Nightingale, used in the largest mGWAS including UK Biobank, quantify about 250 predominantly lipoprotein, lipid, amino-acid and glycolysis-related measures, whereas our catalog rests on 1,955 untargeted Metabolon features that include xenobiotics, nucleotides, peptides and unnamed compounds, and UK Biobank has no urine metabolomics.

Consistent with this, the NMR-based study supported only 4 of our 969 mQTLs and the untargeted MS . study 73, together changing the classification of just 2 loci relative to the nine Metabolon studies when counting any biofluid and any ancestry as reported.
Replication of urine and non-lipid signals therefore requires cohorts with the same platform and biofluid, which is why we combined GCKD with de-novo replication in CRIC.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting our results.

First, European American serum and urine sample sizes were unbalanced; the power-matched analysis shows that the European American biofluid-specificity proportions reflect power, and we therefore base quantitative biofluid comparisons on the balanced African American sample.
Second, ARIC participants were older adults sampled at a single visit, ancestry groups were defined by self-report, and the cohort does not capture the full spectrum of human genetic diversity.
Third, urine mQTLs among African Americans were replicated in CRIC, a chronic kidney disease cohort, whereas replication of African American serum signals relied on the Europeanancestry GCKD study.
Fourth, colocalization and Mendelian randomization support shared genetic effects rather than causality, and candidate causal genes and AlphaGenome predictions require experimental validation.
Our study demonstrates that multi-ancestry, multi-biofluid metabolomics GWAS designs substantially enhance genetic discovery and mechanistic interpretation.

The paired analysis of serum and urine metabolomes revealed complementary genetic architecture, with approximately 75% of metabolites showing biofluid-specific associations in our balanced African American sample.
Trans-ancestry finemapping improved resolution for both shared and population-specific signals, and colocalization with a clinical phenome connected prioritized enzymes and transporters to disease.
The identification of an African Americanenriched splice variant in SLC28A1 illustrates how ancestral diversity can reveal functional variants with potential pharmacogenomic relevance.

As large-scale biobanks and metabolomics platforms continue to expand, integrating data across populations and biofluids will be essential for building a comprehensive atlas of human metabolic genetics.
Our findings provide a template for such integrative approaches and highlight the scientific and equity imperatives for diversifying genomic research.

The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study is a prospective population-based cohort study with enrollment in 1987-1989, recruiting participants aged 45-64 years from four U.S. communities: Forsyth County, North Carolina; Jackson, Mississippi; suburbs of Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Washington County, Maryland. 24, 25 The study was designed to investigate the etiology and natural history of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease.
