text.text: Participants have undergone serial clinical examinations, with the collection of biological specimens at multiple time points.
The present study included ARIC participants with available genotype data and metabolomic profiling from visit 5 (2011-2013).

Serum metabolomic profiling was available for all participants with available blood samples as well as consent while urine profiling was done in in a subsample that did not have previous kidney failure.
This included all African Americans as well as European Americans sampled at the same sample size with oversampling of participants with eGFR<60 mL/min/1.73m 2 .
text.formatted: This included all African Americans as well as European Americans sampled at the same sample size with oversampling of participants with eGFR<60 mL/min/1.73m 2 .

text.text: Participants were stratified by self-reported race/ethnicity into European American (EA) and African American (AA) ancestry groups.

After quality control, the final analytic sample comprised 4,431 participants with metabolite data: EA serum (Nserum = 3,607), EA urine (Nurine = 797), AA serum (Nserum = 818), and AA urine (Nurine = 794).
The study was approved by the institutional review boards at each participating center, and all participants provided written informed consent (IRB00311861).
Genotyping was performed using the Affymetrix Genome-Wide Human SNP Array 6.0 (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA).

Standard quality control procedures were applied, including exclusion of variants if they had call rate <95%, minor allele frequency (MAF) <1%, or significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (P < 1 × 10 -6 ).
text.formatted: Standard quality control procedures were applied, including exclusion of variants if they had call rate <95%, minor allele frequency (MAF) <1%, or significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (P < 1 × 10 -6 ).

text.text: Genotype imputation was performed using the TOPMed Imputation Server (https://imputation.biodatacatalyst.nhlbi.nih.gov/) with the TOPMed r2 reference panel. 52 Phasing was performed with Eagle v2.4 and imputation with Minimac4.
text.formatted: Genotype imputation was performed using the TOPMed Imputation Server (<ref type="url" target="https://imputation.biodatacatalyst.nhlbi.nih.gov/">https://imputation.biodatacatalyst.nhlbi.nih.gov/</ref>) with the TOPMed r2 reference panel. <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> Phasing was performed with Eagle v2.4 and imputation with Minimac4.

text.text: Post-imputation, variants were filtered to retain those with imputation quality (R² ) >0.3 and MAF >1% within each ancestry stratum.
text.formatted: Post-imputation, variants were filtered to retain those with imputation quality (R² ) >0.3 and MAF >1% within each ancestry stratum.

text.text: The TOPMed 21 reference panel includes substantial representation of .
African individuals, enabling improved imputation accuracy and capture of small insertions and deletions (indels) that were poorly represented in earlier reference panels.

Serum and urine metabolites were quantified using the Metabolon HD4 global metabolomics platform (Metabolon, Inc., Durham, NC). 62 This untargeted approach employs ultrahighperformance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) across four complementary ionization methods: two reverse-phase methods using positive ion mode electrospray ionization, one reverse-phase method using negative ion mode electrospray ionization, and one hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) method using negative ion mode electrospray ionization.
text.formatted: Serum and urine metabolites were quantified using the Metabolon HD4 global metabolomics platform (Metabolon, Inc., Durham, NC). <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62</ref> This untargeted approach employs ultrahighperformance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) across four complementary ionization methods: two reverse-phase methods using positive ion mode electrospray ionization, one reverse-phase method using negative ion mode electrospray ionization, and one hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) method using negative ion mode electrospray ionization.

text.text: Metabolites were identified by comparison of retention time, mass-to-charge ratio (m/z), and MS/MS fragmentation patterns to Metabolon's proprietary library of authenticated chemical standards.
Each metabolite was assigned a unique identifier and classified into superpathways (e.g., amino acid, lipid, xenobiotics) and sub-pathways.
Raw metabolite abundance values were normalized to account for inter-day variation by rescaling each compound to set the median equal to 1 across run days.
For serum metabolites, values were rank-based inverse normal transformed.

For urinary metabolites, we applied probabilistic quotient (PQ) normalization to account for differences in urine concentration. 63 Briefly, PQ factors were calculated as the median of the ratios of each metabolite's abundance to a reference spectrum (median of all samples) across 372 endogenous metabolites with <1% missingness.
text.formatted: For urinary metabolites, we applied probabilistic quotient (PQ) normalization to account for differences in urine concentration. <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">63</ref> Briefly, PQ factors were calculated as the median of the ratios of each metabolite's abundance to a reference spectrum (median of all samples) across 372 endogenous metabolites with <1% missingness.

text.text: Urinary metabolite values were divided by the sample-specific PQ factor, then rank-based inverse normal transformed.
Metabolites with >50% missing values were excluded from analysis.
text.formatted: Metabolites with >50% missing values were excluded from analysis.

text.text: Metabolites were retained for genome-wide association analysis if they had measurements in ≥300 participants within an ancestry-biofluid stratum.
The platform quantified a total of 1,316 metabolites in serum and 1,374 metabolites in urine after quality control.

Metabolite annotations were harmonized across biofluids to reflect the newer (=urine) Metabolite annotation, yielding 1,955 unique analytes (581 serum-only, 639 urine-only, 735 detected in both biofluids).
Covariates for GWAS were age, sex and the first 10 principal components of ancestry.
Age was calculated as of the date of visit 5 examination.
Sex was self-reported.
Genetic principal components (PCs) 1-10 were derived from genome-wide genotype data using PLINK v1.9 64 and calculated separately within each ancestry group.
text.formatted: Genetic principal components (PCs) 1-10 were derived from genome-wide genotype data using PLINK v1.9 <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64</ref> and calculated separately within each ancestry group.

text.text: Genome-wide association testing was performed separately within each ancestry-biofluid stratum (EA serum, EA urine, AA serum, AA urine) using REGENIE v3.1. 65 a two-step whole-genome regression approach that accounts for relatedness and population structure while maintaining computational efficiency for biobank-scale data.
text.formatted: Genome-wide association testing was performed separately within each ancestry-biofluid stratum (EA serum, EA urine, AA serum, AA urine) using REGENIE v3.1. <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65</ref> a two-step whole-genome regression approach that accounts for relatedness and population structure while maintaining computational efficiency for biobank-scale data.

text.text: In step 1, a whole-genome regression model was fit using a subset of high-quality genotyped variants (MAF >1%, minor allele count > 100, genotyping rate >90%, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium P > 1 × 10 -15 ).
text.formatted: In step 1, a whole-genome regression model was fit using a subset of high-quality genotyped variants (MAF >1%, minor allele count > 100, genotyping rate >90%, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium P > 1 × 10 -15 ).

text.text: In step 2, association testing was performed for all imputed variants using a linear regression model with the step 1 predictions as an offset.
All association tests were two-sided.
The association model included the following covariates: age, sex, and the first 10 ancestryspecific principal components.
Association testing was restricted to variants with MAF >1% and imputation R² ≥0.3 within each stratum.
text.formatted: Association testing was restricted to variants with MAF >1% and imputation R² ≥0.3 within each stratum.

text.text: Genomic inflation factors (λ) were calculated for each metabolite GWAS to assess residual population stratification or technical artifacts.

African American participants of ARIC show moderate, well-characterized European admixture (median proportion of European ancestry approximately 15%). 66 Association testing within each ancestry stratum, adjustment for ten ancestry-specific genetic principal components and REGENIE's leave-one-chromosome-out whole-genome regression, which captures relatedness and population structure, 65 together account for the global-ancestry variation that admixture generates.
text.formatted: African American participants of ARIC show moderate, well-characterized European admixture (median proportion of European ancestry approximately 15%). <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">66</ref> Association testing within each ancestry stratum, adjustment for ten ancestry-specific genetic principal components and REGENIE's leave-one-chromosome-out whole-genome regression, which captures relatedness and population structure, <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65</ref> together account for the global-ancestry variation that admixture generates.

text.text: Study-wide significance was defined as P < 2.56 × 10 -11 (5 × 10 -8 / 1,955 metabolites), corresponding to a Bonferroni correction for the number of unique metabolites tested.
text.formatted: Study-wide significance was defined as P < 2.56 × 10 -11 (5 × 10 -8 / 1,955 metabolites), corresponding to a Bonferroni correction for the number of unique metabolites tested.

text.text: Metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) were defined by merging significant variants within ±500 kb windows within each ancestry and merging any overlapping windows (Extended Data Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) were defined by merging significant variants within ±500 kb windows within each ancestry and merging any overlapping windows (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Variance explained by index variants was compared across strata descriptively.
Smaller discovery samples detect only larger-effect associations.
Shared mQTLs were defined based on genomic proximity using a 1 Mb window.
Specifically, a locus was considered shared across ancestries if the index variants for the same metabolite and biofluid in both the EA and AA analyses were located within 1 Mb of each other.
Analogously, a locus was considered shared across biofluids if the index variants for the same metabolite in serum and urine were located within 1 Mb of each other.
Per-stratum counts of mQTLs, distinct genomic regions, and metabolites with at least one genome-wide-significant association are provided in Supplementary Table 5.
text.formatted: Per-stratum counts of mQTLs, distinct genomic regions, and metabolites with at least one genome-wide-significant association are provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">5</ref>.

text.text: Loci that did not meet this proximity criterion were classified as biofluid-or candidate ancestry-specific, respectively.

Each of the 632 candidate ancestry-specific mQTLs (590 EA-specific, 42 AA-specific; Supplementary Tables 3 4) was evaluated using a three-step rule to distinguish genuine ancestry-specific effects from those that are more parsimoniously explained as statistically driven, e.g. by imputation availability or power (Extended Data Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Each of the 632 candidate ancestry-specific mQTLs (590 EA-specific, 42 AA-specific; Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">3</ref> <ref type="table">4</ref>) was evaluated using a three-step rule to distinguish genuine ancestry-specific effects from those that are more parsimoniously explained as statistically driven, e.g. by imputation availability or power (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: First, availability: if the index variant, or a proxy at LD r² ≥ 0.8, was not available or did not pass quality control in the other ancestry, the locus was excluded as imputation-driven.

Second, power: for loci passing the availability check, we calculated the power to detect the discovery effect size at the other ancestry's observed sample size and standard error; loci with <80% power were excluded as powerdriven.
text.formatted: Second, power: for loci passing the availability check, we calculated the power to detect the discovery effect size at the other ancestry's observed sample size and standard error; loci with <80% power were excluded as powerdriven.

text.text: Third, heterogeneity: for the remaining loci, we tested for effect-size heterogeneity between ancestries using a two-sided z-test, applying a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold (P < 0.05/632 = 7.9 × 10⁻⁵) to account for the number of loci tested; loci without significant heterogeneity were likewise excluded as statistically driven, and only those with significant heterogeneity were retained and classified as ancestry-specific.
text.formatted: Third, heterogeneity: for the remaining loci, we tested for effect-size heterogeneity between ancestries using a two-sided z-test, applying a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold (P < 0.05/632 = 7.9 × 10⁻⁵) to account for the number of loci tested; loci without significant heterogeneity were likewise excluded as statistically driven, and only those with significant heterogeneity were retained and classified as ancestry-specific.

text.text: Full per-locus statistics (effect sizes and standard errors in both ancestries, power, and heterogeneity Pvalue) for the retained ancestry-specific loci are provided in Supplementary Table 20.
text.formatted: Full per-locus statistics (effect sizes and standard errors in both ancestries, power, and heterogeneity Pvalue) for the retained ancestry-specific loci are provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">20</ref>.

text.text: At the level of statistical fine-mapping, a credible set is termed a fine-mapped ancestry-specific signal if MESuSiE assigns it to one ancestry (PIP > 0.5, with PIP_shared ≤ 0.5) in Supplementary Tables 21 and 23; this applies to every credible set in the dataset, independent of the locuslevel classification above.
text.formatted: At the level of statistical fine-mapping, a credible set is termed a fine-mapped ancestry-specific signal if MESuSiE assigns it to one ancestry (PIP > 0.5, with PIP_shared ≤ 0.5) in Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">21</ref> and <ref type="table">23</ref>; this applies to every credible set in the dataset, independent of the locuslevel classification above.

text.text: Where an mQTL is independently classified as ancestry-specific at both levels, i.e., it passes the locus-level rule above and carries a fine-mapped ancestryspecific signal for the same ancestry, we refer to it as a fine-mapped ancestry-specific mQTL.
We prioritized candidate causal genes for each mQTL based on the ProGeM framework 67 with additional extensions (https://github.com/genepi-freiburg/GWASannotation) 68 .
text.formatted: We prioritized candidate causal genes for each mQTL based on the ProGeM framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">67</ref> with additional extensions (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/genepi-freiburg/GWASannotation">https://github.com/genepi-freiburg/GWASannotation</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">68</ref> .

text.text: The pipeline integrates gene proximity, LD-based gene overlap, functional variant consequences annotated with Ensembl VEP v101, 69 genetic colocalization with cis-eQTL and cis-pQTL datasets, and polygenic priority scores (PoPS). 70 For European American mQTLs, colocalization was performed against cis-eQTLs from GTEx v8 50 and eQTLGen, 71 and against cis-pQTLs from ARIC EA participants. 72 For mQTLs among African Americans, cis-eQTL colocalization used the multi-ancestry Kachuri et al. 73 eQTL resource, and cis-pQTL colocalization used cis-pQTLs from ARIC in AA participants. 72 Colocalization was performed using the coloc.abf function from the coloc R package. 74 We retained signals with evidence for a shared causal variant (PPH4 > 0.8) and suggestive cis-eQTL or cis-pQTL associations (-log₁₀(P) > 5).
text.formatted: The pipeline integrates gene proximity, LD-based gene overlap, functional variant consequences annotated with Ensembl VEP v101, <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">69</ref> genetic colocalization with cis-eQTL and cis-pQTL datasets, and polygenic priority scores (PoPS). <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">70</ref> For European American mQTLs, colocalization was performed against cis-eQTLs from GTEx v8 <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> and eQTLGen, <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">71</ref> and against cis-pQTLs from ARIC EA participants. <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72</ref> For mQTLs among African Americans, cis-eQTL colocalization used the multi-ancestry Kachuri et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73</ref> eQTL resource, and cis-pQTL colocalization used cis-pQTLs from ARIC in AA participants. <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72</ref> Colocalization was performed using the coloc.abf function from the coloc R package. <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">74</ref> We retained signals with evidence for a shared causal variant (PPH4 > 0.8) and suggestive cis-eQTL or cis-pQTL associations (-log₁₀(P) > 5).

text.text: Gene prioritization relied on a weighted scoring scheme.
Proximity to the lead variant was scored as 1.00, 0.99, and 0.98 for the first, second, and third nearest genes, respectively.
Genes overlapping the LD interval received 1.00, and VEP annotations indicating moderate or high impact contributed 1.02.
Cis-eQTL association without evidence of colocalization contributed 0.5.

Colocalization with cis-eQTLs in tissues of interest for metabolism (defined as tissues enriched in paired plasma and urine mGWAS findings 14 , GTEx v8 50 : adrenal gland, heart left ventricle, kidney cortex, liver, pancreas, small intestine terminal ileum, colon transverse, stomach; kidney-specific datasets: tubule and glomeruli) was scored at 1.04, while general cis-eQTL colocalization was scored at 1.03.
text.formatted: Colocalization with cis-eQTLs in tissues of interest for metabolism (defined as tissues enriched in paired plasma and urine mGWAS findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , GTEx v8 50 : adrenal gland, heart left ventricle, kidney cortex, liver, pancreas, small intestine terminal ileum, colon transverse, stomach; kidney-specific datasets: tubule and glomeruli) was scored at 1.04, while general cis-eQTL colocalization was scored at 1.03.

text.text: For AA mQTLs, tissues of interest were not defined separately; colocalization with the Kachuri cis-eQTL resource was scored at 1.03 (general colocalization).
Plasma cis-pQTL colocalization (ARIC PWAS 72 ) was weighted at 1.05.
PoPS scores were computed per locus and ancestry stratum; the gene with the highest PoPS score per locus received an additive weight of 0.5 and the second-highest 0.25.

To evaluate whether reported associations could reflect confounding by other correlated metabolites, we applied a method for covariate selection in multiphenotype studies (CMS) 75 using the authors' reference implementation (CMS_v1.0.
text.formatted: To evaluate whether reported associations could reflect confounding by other correlated metabolites, we applied a method for covariate selection in multiphenotype studies (CMS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">75</ref> using the authors' reference implementation (CMS_v1.0.

text.text: R, function MC()), unmodified.

For each of the 247 prioritized genes in each ancestry-by-biofluid stratum, we took the single most . strongly associated (target metabolite, index variant) pair (366 gene-by-stratum combinations) and offered as candidate covariates the 50 metabolites most correlated with the target (|r| ≤ 0.8; measured in ≥90% of subjects with the target measured; remaining missingness mean-imputed).
We derived an equivalent sample-size increase (SSincr) as the ratio of CMS-adjusted to marginal -log₁₀P (Supplementary Table 12).
text.formatted: We derived an equivalent sample-size increase (SSincr) as the ratio of CMS-adjusted to marginal -log₁₀P (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">12</ref>).

text.text: Multi-ancestry finemapping was performed using MESuSiE (Multi-ancestry Sum of Single Effects), 35 which extends the Sum of Single Effects (SuSiE) 76 model to jointly analyze GWAS summary statistics from multiple ancestries.
text.formatted: Multi-ancestry finemapping was performed using MESuSiE (Multi-ancestry Sum of Single Effects), <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> which extends the Sum of Single Effects (SuSiE) <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">76</ref> model to jointly analyze GWAS summary statistics from multiple ancestries.

text.text: MESuSiE explicitly models both shared and ancestry-specific causal signals using a mixture of bivariate normal distributions, allowing identification of variants with effects in one or both ancestries.
For each mQTL region, we provided ancestry-specific GWAS summary statistics (effect estimates and standard errors) and LD matrices calculated from the ARIC genotype data.
For comparison, single-ancestry finemapping was performed using SuSiE 76 separately within EA and AA strata based on the same set of shared variants.
text.formatted: For comparison, single-ancestry finemapping was performed using SuSiE <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">76</ref> separately within EA and AA strata based on the same set of shared variants.

text.text: SuSiE decomposes the genetic signal into a sum of single-effect vectors, each representing one causal variant, and outputs posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs) for each variant and 95% credible sets for each independent signal.
Finemapping was performed for the genomic windows harboring mQTLs in serum and urine separately based on a harmonized cross-ancestry SNP set with joint variants.
For shared loci, the window with the lowest P value across EA and AA was selected for joint multi-ancestry finemapping with MESuSiE.
Multi-ancestry fine-mapping with MESuSiE was run on all 800 unique region-metabolite pairs (629 serum, 171 urine).

For 6 of these (2 serum, 4 urine), MESuSiE returned no credible set, likely reflecting the absence of a remaining genome-wide significant variant (P < 5 × 10⁻⁸/1955 = 2.56 × 10⁻¹¹) within the harmonized cross-ancestry SNP set.
text.formatted: For 6 of these (2 serum, 4 urine), MESuSiE returned no credible set, likely reflecting the absence of a remaining genome-wide significant variant (P < 5 × 10⁻⁸/1955 = 2.56 × 10⁻¹¹) within the harmonized cross-ancestry SNP set.

text.text: Credible sets were therefore obtained for 794 regionmetabolite pairs (627 serum, 167 urine).
Single-ancestry finemapping with SuSiE was performed on the original per-ancestry windows, but based on the harmonized cross-ancestry SNP set to be comparable to MESuSiE.
Multi-allelic variants were excluded from finemapping analyses to ensure consistent LD estimation.
Credible sets were classified as ancestry-shared (PIPshared > 0.5), EA-specific (PIPEA > 0.5 and PIPshared ≤ 0.5), or AA-specific (PIPAA > 0.5 and PIPshared ≤ 0.5).
text.formatted: Credible sets were classified as ancestry-shared (PIPshared > 0.5), EA-specific (PIPEA > 0.5 and PIPshared ≤ 0.5), or AA-specific (PIPAA > 0.5 and PIPshared ≤ 0.5).

text.text: Variants were considered high-. predicted effect relative to common variants in gnomAD v3 (MAF > 1%).
text.formatted: Variants were considered high-. predicted effect relative to common variants in gnomAD v3 (MAF > 1%).

text.text: Variant-level summaries were generated by retaining the strongest predicted effect across all tracks, as well as separately for metabolically relevant tissues (defined as tissues enriched in paired plasma and urine mGWAS findings 14 : kidney, liver, adrenal gland, heart left ventricle, pancreas, small intestine terminal ileum, colon transverse, stomach).

Variants with quantile scores exceeding 0.99 were considered to have reliably predicted functional effects and are reported as highconfidence, consistent with the model's reported concordance with observed eQTL effect sizes at this threshold (Spearman r ≈ 0.73).
In addition to the collapsed annotation in the supplementary tables, all individual annotations are provided in Supplementary Data 2.
AlphaGenome annotation was performed using Python 3.12.3 and alphagenome v0.6.1.

AlphaGenome predictions are in-silico, hypothesis-generating annotations of potential regulatory consequence; they were not experimentally validated in this study and are reported as supporting evidence for gene and variant prioritization.

Genetic differentiation between European (CEU) and West African (YRI) reference populations was quantified using Fst, obtained from PopHuman's 79 precomputed Fst_CEU2YRI_10kb track, which reports values in non-overlapping 10-kb windows (hg19).
text.formatted: Genetic differentiation between European (CEU) and West African (YRI) reference populations was quantified using Fst, obtained from PopHuman's <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">79</ref> precomputed Fst_CEU2YRI_10kb track, which reports values in non-overlapping 10-kb windows (hg19).

text.text: Index variant positions were converted from GRCh38 to GRCh37/hg19.

For 609 of the 969 (63%) mQTL index variants, the Fst value of the overlapping window was extracted using the rtracklayer R package, and expressed as a percentile relative to the genome-wide Fst distribution together with a onesided empirical P-value (the proportion of genome-wide Fst values greater than or equal to the observed value).

Index variants falling in a gap between windows have no Fst value, a property of the non-contiguous window track that was not further resolved; this applied to 37% of mQTLs and reflects window coverage rather than a systematic bias by locus type.

To test whether apparent biofluid-specific biology in the European-American (EA) stratum reflects the larger serum sample size (N = 3,607) relative to urine (N = 797), we repeated the complete EA serum mGWAS restricted to the 797 EA participants who also contributed urine measurements.

Gene set, pathway, and tissue enrichment analyses (GO, KEGG, GTEx tissue, . and Metabolon super-/sub-pathway) were repeated on this power-matched locus set using the identical pipeline as the primary enrichment analysis.

Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway database. 80 Enrichment was assessed using one-sided Fisher's exact tests comparing the proportion of mQTL-implicated genes in each pathway to the genomic background.
text.formatted: Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway database. <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">80</ref> Enrichment was assessed using one-sided Fisher's exact tests comparing the proportion of mQTL-implicated genes in each pathway to the genomic background.

text.text: Pathways with fewer than 3 mapped genes were excluded.
Fold enrichment was defined as the ratio of the fraction of mQTL-implicated genes in a pathway to the fraction of background genes in that pathway.

To identify tissue-specific gene sets for enrichment analyses, we used pre-compiled lists of the top 10% of specifically expressed genes across GTEx V8 tissues and human and murine kidney cell types, derived as described previously. 7 Briefly, tissue-specific expression was assessed by ranking genes by t-statistics from a linear model comparing expression in each tissue or cell type to all others, following the approach of Finucane et al. 81 The resulting top 10% gene lists per tissue were used as the basis for enrichment testing against our identified metaboliteassociated genes.
text.formatted: To identify tissue-specific gene sets for enrichment analyses, we used pre-compiled lists of the top 10% of specifically expressed genes across GTEx V8 tissues and human and murine kidney cell types, derived as described previously. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> Briefly, tissue-specific expression was assessed by ranking genes by t-statistics from a linear model comparing expression in each tissue or cell type to all others, following the approach of Finucane et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">81</ref> The resulting top 10% gene lists per tissue were used as the basis for enrichment testing against our identified metaboliteassociated genes.

text.text: Gene set overrepresentation was tested analogously to KEGG.
Of the 220 and 81 genes associated in serum and urine (overlap: 54), respectively, we were able to map 220 and 80 to the KEGG annotated genes.
KEGG enrichment was performed using clusterprofiler and KEGG.db v3.2.4.
Pathway enrichment regarding annotated sub-and super-pathways as annotated by Metabolon Inc., was performed using Fisher's exact tests.
In all enrichment analyses, statistical significance was determined by a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold accounting for the number of pathways/gene sets in the background, respectively.
We assessed novelty of our 969 mQTLs against eleven published metabolite GWAS: nine Metabolon-annotated studies (Schlosser et al.

(GCKD) 14 , Chen et al. 6 , Long et al. 4 , Yin et al. 20 , Hysi et al. 26 , Lotta et al. 27 , Surendran et al. 5 , Shin et al. 3 , Luo et al. 16 ) and, as secondary-tier evidence, two studies on other platforms (Tambets et al. 2 , Nuclear Magnetic Resonance; Tahir et al. 18 , untargeted Mass Spectrometry) treated as a secondary tier.
text.formatted: (GCKD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , Chen et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> , Long et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , Yin et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> , Hysi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> , Lotta et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> , Surendran et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> , Shin et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> , Luo et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> ) and, as secondary-tier evidence, two studies on other platforms (Tambets et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> , Nuclear Magnetic Resonance; Tahir et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> , untargeted Mass Spectrometry) treated as a secondary tier.

text.text: A locus was called known . if the comparison study reported its own genome-wide-significant (P ≤ 5 × 10⁻⁸) index variant for the same metabolite within ±500 kb of the ARIC index variant, on the same chromosome, and all reported summary statistics are the comparison study's own values for its own variant.

Metabolite identity was matched using, for the primary tier, any concordant match among global Metabolon chemical ID, biofluid-specific chemical ID, or normalized biochemical name; for the secondary tier, normalized name only, supplemented for Tahir by an external-identifier bridge (PubChem, then KEGG, then HMDB; unambiguous 1:1 mappings only).

Looking at biofluid-and ancestry-matched Metabolon-studies served as our primary novelty measure; counting a report in any biofluid and ancestry in all 11 studies as known served as a conservative bound.
Full per-locus results across both definitions are provided in Supplementary Table 9.
text.formatted: Full per-locus results across both definitions are provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">9</ref>.

text.text: As a targeted replication analysis, we additionally evaluated the validation rate of our mQTLs against GCKD specifically -the only other study with a paired serum-and-urine design.

For index variants not found directly in GCKD's summary statistics, we searched for an LD proxy (r² ≥ 0.8, 1000 Genomes European reference panel: CEU, TSI, FIN, GBR, IBS) using LDlinkR, with allele phasing resolved via LDproxy's correlated-alleles output, and used the proxy variant's association statistics in its place.
We then tested for concordant direction of effect at Bonferroni-corrected significance (P < 0.05/# lookups per biofluid) among all directly or proxy-matched pairs.
text.formatted: We then tested for concordant direction of effect at Bonferroni-corrected significance (P < 0.05/# lookups per biofluid) among all directly or proxy-matched pairs.

text.text: Cross-ancestry and cross-biofluid consistency was assessed by comparing effect estimates between strata.
Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated for effect sizes of shared mQTLs.
For visualization, a regression slope was computed as the unweighted mean of the two per-direction regression slopes (regressing y on x and x on y), correcting for discovery-related winner's curse.

As no published Metabolon urine resource exists for African American participants, we obtained de-novo replication in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC), a prospective cohort of Black participants with mild-to-moderate chronic kidney disease recruited across seven U.S. clinical centers. 28, 29 Of 1,514 Black participants with baseline urinary metabolomics, 1,323 additionally had complete covariates and genome-wide genotyping and were included in this replication.
text.formatted: As no published Metabolon urine resource exists for African American participants, we obtained de-novo replication in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC), a prospective cohort of Black participants with mild-to-moderate chronic kidney disease recruited across seven U.S. clinical centers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> Of 1,514 Black participants with baseline urinary metabolomics, 1,323 additionally had complete covariates and genome-wide genotyping and were included in this replication.

text.text: Urinary metabolites were profiled from baseline 24-hour urine samples on the same Metabolon UPLC-MS/MS platform as ARIC and quantified by area-under-the-curve against a library of authenticated standards.

Metabolites were normalized using probabilistic quotient normalization: a reference set of metabolites with <50% missingness, excluding xenobiotics . and unnamed compounds, was used to compute a per-sample scaling factor, followed by median-scaling across samples; each target metabolite was then rank-based inverse-normal transformed.
text.formatted: Metabolites were normalized using probabilistic quotient normalization: a reference set of metabolites with <50% missingness, excluding xenobiotics . and unnamed compounds, was used to compute a per-sample scaling factor, followed by median-scaling across samples; each target metabolite was then rank-based inverse-normal transformed.

text.text: Genotyping was performed in 1,447 participants using the Illumina HumanOmni1-Quad BeadChip and imputed via the Michigan Imputation Server using the TOPMed r2 reference panel (GRCh38).
Covariates were age, sex, study site, and 10 genetic principal components; a sensitivity model additionally adjusted for eGFR (2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation without race, 82 logtransformed).

Of the 109 AA-urine mQTLs identified in ARIC (77 unique index variants, 101 unique metabolites), all 77 index variants were available in CRIC's imputed genotype data at high quality (minimum Minimac R² = 0.950); 94 of 101 metabolites were measured in CRIC, yielding 102 testable variant-metabolite pairs.

Association testing used REGENIE v3.2 65 in two steps: a whole-genome regression model fitted on quality-controlled, LD-pruned genome-wide variants to generate leave-one-chromosome-out predictions for each metabolite, followed by extraction of the 77 index variants with PLINK 2 and single-variant association testing conditional on the step-1 predictions, under the primary and eGFR-adjusted models described above.

text.text: To test whether pharmacologically reduced ACE activity alters fibrinopeptide fragment levels, we performed two individual-level observational analyses in ARIC.

RASi medication use (ACE inhibitor, angiotensin-receptor blocker, and/or aldosterone antagonist in the past 4 weeks) was defined at Visit 5, versus no antihypertensive medication as the comparator; sensitivity analyses isolated each drug class individually and added a third, non-RASi-medication comparator group.

Models were adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI, eGFR (CKD-EPI creatinine equation), diabetes medication use, smoking, and statin use, in the combined EA+AA sample (primary) and each ancestry separately.

The first analysis tested seven clinically measured coagulation markers at Visit 1 (N = 4,122-4,209 per marker), with factor VII and fibrinogen also available at Visit 3 (N = 306); Visit 5 itself had no directly measured coagulation markers.
These markers were therefore measured about two decades before medication ascertainment.

The second analysis tested the same fibrinopeptide fragments plus aspartate, glycylvaline, aspartylaspartate, and serum potassium, all measured contemporaneously at Visit 5 (metabolite values rank-based inverse-normal transformed; potassium on its native scale).
Associations were tested by multivariable linear regression.

To determine whether SLC16A9's colocalization with urate-related traits and coronary atherosclerosis (CAD) reflects one or two separable pathways, we performed two-sample MR for urate (CKDGen Round 4 83 , European ancestry) and five SLC16A9-linked acylcarnitines (carnitine, acetylcarnitine, propionylcarnitine, phenylacetylcarnitine, butyrylcarnitine; ARIC and Shin et al. 3 ) against gout (CKDGen) and CAD (CARDIoGRAMplusC4D 84 ).

text.text: To test gout itself, rather than continuous urate, as a cause of CAD, we performed an additional MR using a casecontrol gout diagnosis GWAS (CKDGen R4) against CAD outcome with CARDIoGRAMplusC4D.

text.text: Repeating this enrichment analysis on the power-matched EA serum data (N=797) recovered the core biological signal at reduced power: 4 of 6 significant GTEx tissues were retained (liver, kidney cortex, small intestine and kidney medulla), 18 of 25 testable KEGG pathways were retained (3 pathways became untestable), with xenobiotic/drug-metabolism, bile secretion, and steroid-hormone-biosynthesis themes remaining robust while most individual amino-acid catabolism pathways (tryptophan, phenylalanine, valine/leucine/isoleucine, beta-alanine) lost significance.
Sub-pathway resolution was far more power-sensitive, with only 1 of 9 fullsample-significant sub-pathways (Fatty Acid, Dicarboxylate) remaining significant.

Broad pathway-level conclusions are therefore largely robust to the EA serum-urine power imbalance, while finer-grained pathway claims should be interpreted with this caveat (Supplementary Tables independent signals when compared to ancestry-specific finemapping using the same model (SuSiE, Methods; Fig 5a, Extended Data Fig 8).
We were able to narrow down many of the EA credible sets by incorporation of evidence from the AA sample -even for the serum analysis with the larger EA sample size (Fig 5c).

Multi-ancestry finemapping improved credible set resolution compared to single-ancestry SuSiE (median set size: 2 vs. ≥6), with AA-specific regions showing the smallest sets, likely reflecting shorter linkage disequilibrium blocks (mean signals per region: 1.95 vs.
